faqs.question: How do you say happy Halloween in French?
faqs.answer: Say "Joyeux Halloween!", roughly zhwah-YUH ah-loh-WEEN. Larousse and the OQLF both class Halloween as feminine, so the by-the-book form is "Joyeuse Halloween!", which is the safer choice for someone in Quebec.

faqs.question: Is Halloween masculine or feminine in French?
faqs.answer: Feminine, according to both Larousse in France and the Office québécois de la langue française. The masculine "Joyeux Halloween" is still what most learner guides teach, so nobody will be confused by either.

faqs.question: How do you say trick or treat in French?
faqs.answer: Wiktionary records "Des bonbons ou un sort!" (treats or a spell) and "Farce ou friandise!" (a trick or a treat). I found no dictionary entry for the singular "un bonbon ou un sort", so use the plural.

faqs.question: Should I use tu or vous in a Halloween message to my boss?
faqs.answer: Use whatever you already use with them, which for most managers is vous. A 2025 Actes Sémiotiques paper argues that an unexpected switch between tu and vous jolts the other person, so a holiday is not the moment to change.

faqs.question: Do people in France actually celebrate Halloween?
faqs.answer: Some do, mostly families with small children. Historian Adrien Lherm dates a boom from 1997 to 2000, with sales near 500 million francs in 2000, and a retreat from 2001 that left it mainly to young children in provincial towns.

faqs.question: Is trick-or-treating common in Quebec?
faqs.answer: Yes. The OQLF's own definition of Halloween has children dressing up and going door to door for treats, and the Ville de Montréal published candy-route ideas for its Ville-Marie borough on 2 October 2026.

faqs.question: Can I say joyeuse Toussaint on 1 November?
faqs.answer: No. Toussaint, All Saints' Day, is a public holiday in France that anticipates the day of the dead on 2 November, so it is not a festive greeting. Wish someone "bon week-end" instead.

faqs.question: What is a cute French Halloween message for a child?
faqs.answer: Try "Joyeux Halloween, mon petit fantôme!" (Happy Halloween, my little ghost). Always use tu with a child and keep it cute: no blood, gore or threats.

faqs.question: What is a short French Halloween caption for Instagram?
faqs.answer: "Mode sorcière activé." (Witch mode on) or "Zéro farce, que des friandises." (Zero tricks, only treats) both fit under a photo. Both are original lines from this page.

faqs.question: Can I make the SubhSandesh Halloween card entirely in French?
faqs.answer: Only partly. The fields you type, such as the letter, the carved word and the closing question of up to 60 characters, can be French, but the interface buttons are English. For a recipient who reads no English, a handwritten French card is better.

# Halloween Wishes in French: 45 Joyeux Halloween Messages

The simplest of all Halloween wishes in French is *Joyeux Halloween!* (zhwah-YUH ah-loh-WEEN). Use *tu* lines for a partner, friends and children, and *vous* lines for colleagues. Keep it short: across SubhSandesh, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone and each page averages 11.1 views.

Below are 45 original wishes with glosses, sorted by recipient. Then come vocabulary, Quebec usage and why France shrugs at 31 October.

## Is it "Joyeux" or "Joyeuse" Halloween?

The dictionaries make the noun feminine. [Larousse lists Halloween](https://www.larousse.fr/dictionnaires/francais/Halloween/38914) as *nom féminin singulier*, and the [Office québécois de la langue française](https://vitrinelinguistique.oqlf.gouv.qc.ca/fiche-gdt/fiche/8398771/halloween) (fiche updated 2022) gives the example *Joyeuse Halloween!*

The real difference is the article. Per the OQLF, Europe says *C'est Halloween!* and Quebec *C'est l'Halloween!*, and the silent *h* elides, as in *bonbons d'Halloween*.

Learner guides mostly teach *Joyeux Halloween*, and nobody in France will blink at it. For Quebec, *Joyeuse Halloween* is safer.

## Tu or vous: which register for a Halloween message?

*Tu* is informal; *vous* is formal or plural. Use *tu* with a partner, friends, family and children, and *vous* with a manager, teacher or neighbour you vouvoie.

Do not switch just because it is Halloween. In a 2025 *Actes Sémiotiques* paper, [Verónica Estay Stange and Marika Nesi Lammardo argue](https://www.unilim.fr/actes-semiotiques/9162) that once *tu* or *vous* is the norm between two people, an unexpected switch "jolts" the other. Follow whatever you already do.

## 45 French Halloween wishes, by recipient

Every line is original and glossed. For a woman, adjust gendered endings.

### 1. Short text messages (tu)

For a quick WhatsApp. Each is under 15 words.

- **Joyeux Halloween! Je t'envoie un fantôme, il est gentil.** ("I'm sending you a ghost; he's friendly.")
- **Ne mange pas tous les bonbons d'un coup ce soir!** ("Don't eat every sweet at once tonight!")
- **Trente et un octobre : sors ton balai et ta meilleure grimace.** ("31 October: broom out, scariest face on.")
- **Que ta citrouille brille plus fort que celle des voisins!** ("May your pumpkin outshine the neighbours'!")
- **Une petite sorcière m'a demandé de te souhaiter un joyeux Halloween.** ("A little witch asked me to wish you happy Halloween.")
- **Plein de bonbons et zéro frayeur pour toi!** ("Lots of sweets and zero frights for you!")
- **Attention : les chats noirs ont tous ton adresse.** ("Careful: the black cats all have your address.")

### 2. For a partner (tu)

Romantic but clean. *Mon cœur* (mohn KUR) means "sweetheart".

- **Joyeux Halloween, mon cœur. Tu es le seul fantôme qui me hante.** ("No ghost haunts me except you.")
- **Avec toi, même une maison hantée ressemble à un chez-nous.** ("With you, even a haunted house feels like home.")
- **Tu m'as jeté un sort, et je ne cherche pas l'antidote.** ("You bewitched me, and I want no antidote.")
- **Ma citrouille préférée, c'est toi.** ("My favourite pumpkin is you.")
- **Ce soir je suis en vampire, mais c'est toi qui m'as volé le cœur.** ("Tonight I'm in vampire gear, yet you stole my heart.")
- **Une potion, deux chats noirs et toi : ma soirée parfaite.** ("A potion, two black cats and you: my perfect evening.")
- **Si tu entends frapper trois fois ce soir, c'est moi.** ("If you hear three knocks tonight, it's me.")

### 3. For friends (tu)

Teasing works here. *Complice* (kohm-PLEESS) suits either gender.

- **Joyeux Halloween à mon complice de toujours!** ("To my accomplice, now and always!")
- **On se déguise en quoi? J'ai une idée qui va te faire hurler.** ("Costume plans? Mine will make you scream.")
- **Les fantômes passent, les vrais amis restent.** ("Ghosts come and go; real friends stay.")
- **Toi, moi, un film d'horreur et des bonbons : vingt heures?** ("You, me, a horror film and sweets: eight o'clock?")
- **Je partage mes bonbons avec toi : vraie preuve d'amitié.** ("I'm sharing my sweets: true proof of friendship.")
- **Rappel : c'est toi qui as crié le plus fort l'an dernier.** ("Reminder: you screamed loudest last year.")
- **Ta grimace de zombie reste la meilleure de la bande.** ("Your zombie face is still the gang's best.")

### 4. For family (tu, and one vous)

Families mostly say *tu*. Some say *vous* to grandparents, as in the last line.

- **Joyeux Halloween, maman! Merci pour tous ces costumes cousus en urgence.** ("Thanks, Mum, for all those emergency costumes.")
- **Papa, cette année tu distribues les bonbons, sans les goûter.** ("Dad, you hand out sweets this year, untasted.")
- **Joyeux Halloween, petit frère : je surveille ton sac de bonbons.** ("Little brother, I'm watching your sweet bag.")
- **Gros bisous de tous vos petits monstres!** ("Big kisses from all your little monsters!")
- **Mamie, vous aviez raison : la soupe au potiron bat tous les bonbons.** ("Grandma, you were right: pumpkin soup beats any sweet.")

### 5. For colleagues and neighbours (vous)

Short and warm. *Vous* is also plural, so one line covers a team.

- **Je vous souhaite une excellente soirée d'Halloween.** ("I wish you an excellent Halloween evening.")
- **Très bon Halloween à vous et à votre famille!** ("A very happy Halloween to you and your family!")
- **Les bonbons sont sur mon bureau, servez-vous. Bon Halloween!** ("The sweets are on my desk; help yourselves.")
- **Merci pour cette semaine; ce soir, place aux citrouilles.** ("Thanks for this week; tonight, pumpkins take over.")
- **Bonne soirée d'Halloween, et bon week-end de la Toussaint.** ("Good Halloween, and a good All Saints' weekend.")
- **Les enfants passeront peut-être sonner : merci de votre accueil.** ("The kids may ring tonight: thanks for welcoming them.")
- **Bonne fête de l'Halloween!** ("Happy Halloween!", Quebec style.)

### 6. For kids (tu)

Always *tu* with a child. Cute, never gory.

- **Joyeux Halloween, mon petit fantôme!** ("Happy Halloween, my little ghost!")
- **Tu fais une sorcière très rigolote.** ("You make a very funny witch.")
- **Ce soir, tous les monstres sont gentils, promis.** ("Tonight every monster is kind, promise.")
- **Un bonbon pour toi, un pour moi, puis brossage de dents.** ("One sweet for you, one for me, then teeth.")
- **Des bonbons ou un sort? Pour toi, des bonbons.** ("Treats or a spell? For you, treats.")

### 7. Card lines and captions

The first three suit a card. The last four are Instagram captions.

- **Que cette nuit du 31 octobre vous apporte plus de rires que de frissons.** ("May 31 October bring more laughs than shivers.")
- **Une citrouille, une bougie et tous mes vœux pour un joyeux Halloween.** ("A pumpkin, a candle and all my best wishes.")
- **À la lueur des citrouilles, je pense bien à toi.** ("By pumpkin light, I'm thinking of you.")
- **Bien déguisés, mal maquillés, très contents.** ("Well costumed, badly made up, very happy.")
- **Mode sorcière activé.** ("Witch mode on.")
- **Notre équipe de fantômes au complet.** ("Our full ghost squad.")
- **Zéro farce, que des friandises.** ("Zero tricks, only treats.")

## French Halloween vocabulary, checked against Larousse

Five words carry most of these lines. Senses are Larousse's; pronunciations are approximate.

- **citrouille** (see-TROO-yuh), n.f.: pumpkin; also slang for a big head.
- **sorcière** (sor-SYAIR), n.f.: fairy-tale witch; also an insult for a woman.
- **fantôme** (fahn-TOHM), n.m.: a dead person's apparition.
- **bonbon** (bohn-BOHN), n.m.: a cooked-sugar sweet.
- **sort** (SOR), n.m.: a harmful spell, as in *jeter un sort*.

For "trick or treat", Wiktionary records *Des bonbons ou un sort!* and *Farce ou friandise!* I found no dictionary entry for the singular *un bonbon ou un sort*, so use the plural.

The table compares the five greetings you will most need. Each row shows register and best fit.

| French phrase | English meaning | Register | Best use |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Joyeux Halloween!* | Happy Halloween! | Neutral | Anyone in France |
| *Joyeuse Halloween!* | Happy Halloween! (OQLF form, 2022) | Neutral | Anyone in Quebec |
| *Excellente soirée d'Halloween!* | Have an excellent Halloween evening! | Formal vous | Colleague, neighbour |
| *Des bonbons ou un sort!* | Treats or a spell! | Playful tu | Kids, door-to-door |
| *Bonne fête de l'Halloween!* | Happy Halloween! (with article) | Neutral | Quebec office or class |

The greeting barely changes. The article and *tu*/*vous* show you know their French.

## How France and Quebec celebrate 31 October differently

In Quebec, trick-or-treating is ordinary: the OQLF defines Halloween as children dressing up and going door to door for treats. A [Ville de Montréal notice of 2 October 2026](https://montreal.ca/actualites/lhalloween-dans-ville-marie-99427) suggests ways to improve your *parcours de cueillette de bonbons* (candy route).

France is different. Historian Adrien Lherm's chapter [*Halloween et les Français*](https://books.openedition.org/psorbonne/43378) (2010) records a failed Printemps Haussmann stand in 1993, then a 1997–2000 boom: France Télécom covered the Trocadéro gardens with over 7,000 pumpkins, and Halloween sales passed 250 million francs in 1998 and neared 500 million in 2000.

The retreat began in 2001, which Lherm blames mainly on the post-9/11 slump rather than Catholic counter-campaigns. By 2006 the press called it dead, though small children in provincial towns kept it alive.

### Toussaint on 1 November

The next day is Toussaint, All Saints' Day, and [Service-public.fr lists 1 November](https://www.service-public.fr/particuliers/vosdroits/F2405) as a public holiday. Larousse adds that it anticipates the day of the dead on 2 November, so wish *bon week-end*, never *joyeuse Toussaint*.

## Sending a French wish on an interactive Halloween card

For one person, put your French on the [interactive Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween). It takes a letter, up to six photos and the word they carve into the pumpkin; the closing question is editable up to 60 characters, so *Veux-tu être mon fantôme préféré?* fits.

One honest limit: the interface is English, so for a recipient who reads no English a handwritten French card wins. Across SubhSandesh, 90.9% of started pages get published and shared (platform-wide, not Halloween data).

For a partner who should hear your accent, the [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) adds a voice note up to 60 seconds. Neither page is a party tool; both are for one recipient.

## When a French Halloween wish is the wrong move

Skip the jokes with anyone grieving near 1 and 2 November. Older relatives may see Halloween as a commercial import: Lherm records bishops protesting from 1999 and a *Comité Non à Halloween* in Dijon. With a colleague you barely know, one *vous* line in an email beats any card.

## Sources

- Larousse, dictionary entries.
- OQLF, *Grand dictionnaire terminologique*, 2022.
- Estay Stange and Nesi Lammardo, *Actes Sémiotiques*, 2025.
- Ville de Montréal, 2 October 2026.
- Lherm, Éditions de la Sorbonne, 2010.
- Service-public.fr, checked 1 January 2026.
- Wiktionary.
